title: mem_closure_pair_iff — The Elementary Bridge
content: Membership in the additive submonoid generated by {m, n} is exactly being a nonnegative integer combination a·m + b·n. Derived from Mathlib's `AddSubmonoid.mem_closure_pair` (`c ∈ closure {a,b} ↔ ∃ m n, m • a + n • b = c`) by rewriting the ℕ-scalar action `•` to multiplication via `smul_eq_mul`. This is the lemma that lets the canonical closure-based statement be read in the elementary `a·m + b·n` language of the parent gallery entry.
mathContext: $k \in \langle m, n \rangle_{+} \iff \exists a, b \in \mathbb{N}.\ a m + b n = k$

title: sylvester_frobenius_canonical — Mathlib's Canonical Predicate
content: The Chicken McNugget theorem on canonical footing: for coprime m, n > 1, `FrobeniusNumber (m*n - m - n) {m, n}`. Here `FrobeniusNumber k s := IsGreatest { j | j ∉ AddSubmonoid.closure s } k`, so the single predicate encodes both 'm·n − m − n is not representable' and 'it is the greatest such'. The proof is a re-export of Mathlib's verified `frobeniusNumber_pair`. Unlike the parent entry's homemade `Representable`/`frobeniusNumber`, the extremal claim here is inherited from the general theory.

title: frobenius_not_in_closure / above_frobenius_in_closure
content: Splitting the canonical `IsGreatest` claim with `frobeniusNumber_iff` yields the two halves of Sylvester's theorem: the Frobenius value m·n − m − n is itself not in the closure (not representable), and every integer strictly above it is in the closure (representable). Each half is independently useful and each transfers to the elementary combination language via the Part I bridge.
mathContext: $mn-m-n \notin \langle m,n\rangle_{+}$ and $\forall k > mn-m-n,\ k \in \langle m,n\rangle_{+}$

title: frobenius_not_representable / above_frobenius_representable
content: Composing the canonical theorem (Part II) with the elementary bridge (Part I) gives the corollaries in the same `a·m + b·n` language as the parent gallery entry — but now machine-checked against Mathlib's verified development: m·n − m − n is not of the form a·m + b·n, and every larger integer is.
mathContext: $\neg\,\exists a,b.\ am+bn = mn-m-n \quad\text{and}\quad \forall k > mn-m-n,\ \exists a,b.\ am+bn=k$

title: Chicken McNugget Instance g(3, 5) = 7
content: Instantiating m = 3, n = 5 gives the classic example: 7 = 3·5 − 3 − 5 is the canonical `FrobeniusNumber 7 {3, 5}`, 7 cannot be made from 3s and 5s (¬∃ a b, 3a + 5b = 7), and every amount above 7 can be (∀ k > 7, ∃ a b, 3a + 5b = k). Coprimality of 3 and 5 is discharged by `decide` (kernel reduction), keeping the entry axiom-free.
